opening.headline: When you make multiple changes at the same time and don't know what was effective, learn how to design an experiment to isolate and compare the change factors.
body: I changed the prompt, added examples, cleaned up the data, and even changed the model version, and the results improved. However, I don't know what changes are due to this. Even when the results worsen, the cause cannot be reversed, and there is no basis for applying the same treatment elsewhere.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the concepts of variable control and comparison group, the construction of an experimental table that applies changes one by one, and the limitations of reproducibility and interpretation of results. Next, the instructor explains a case where it is impossible to reach a conclusion by changing three things at once, and the process of separating them and returning them.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can distinguish between experimental designs that isolate factors of change
Can determine the limits of interpretation of experimental results

screens.title: I made several changes at the same time and don't know what worked.
screens.lead: Read the history of one team's improvement efforts. The results have improved, but it is good to read while thinking about why it is difficult.

paragraphs: One team worked on several tasks throughout the week to improve response quality. We fixed the prompts, added examples, cleaned up the training data, and changed the model version. When I finally ran the evaluation, the results were improving.

This is great news, but questions remain. Which of the four changes worked? If you don't know, you won't be able to apply the same improvement to another feature next week or know which changes to revert if the results go south.
Improvements whose cause cannot be explained cannot be used in the next task. This class covers experimental design, which involves isolating changes to find out which ones worked.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Proving improvement is one thing, but knowing the cause of the improvement is another. You need both.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the current way of working.

screens.title: Think about a time when you changed several things at once.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever changed several things at once? At that time, were you able to explain the results by breaking them down into changes?
items.answer: It's common to change several things at once when you're short on time. However, if the results cannot be explained change-by-change, it is impossible to know whether the improvement was coincidental or inevitable.

items.prompt: Did you keep it the way it was before changing it?
items.answer: If you don't save the state before changing it, you won't be able to recreate the baseline. The premise of the comparison is to keep prompts, data versions, and settings as they were before any changes.

items.prompt: Was it possible to run it again with the same evaluation set and settings?
items.answer: If settings are not recorded, they cannot be reproduced, and unreproducible results are difficult to use as a basis for comparison. Reproducibility is covered in detail later.

screens.outro: Let's look at two principles for isolating change: variable control and comparison groups.

screens.title: Variable control and comparison group
screens.lead: Click the next button to check the basic principles of comparative experiments one by one.

visual.alt: A cyclical illustration of starting from a baseline, applying changes one by one, and repeating the evaluation.
labels: Reevaluate using the same evaluation set, same grader, and same settings.

steps.title: variable control
steps.body: Change just one factor you want to compare and keep everything else fixed. Only then can we attribute the difference in results to that one factor. If you change both things at the same time, you cannot split the difference.

steps.title: comparison group
steps.body: Run the baseline together without changing anything. You must have a comparison group to determine whether the value after the change is due to the change or just a change from that day.

steps.title: Things to pin
steps.body: We use the same evaluation set, same scorer, and same sampling settings. If any part of the evaluation environment is different, it is impossible to know whether the difference in values ​​is due to the change or the environment.

steps.title: cycle of experimentation
steps.body: You cycle through the evaluation, see why it was wrong, come up with a hypothesis, make a change, and evaluate again. Looking at the results and moving on to the next hypothesis is the basic unit of improvement. At the end of one cycle, the baseline is updated and used as the starting point for the next cycle.

steps.title: Generalization check
steps.body: Separate data used during the experiment from data for final verification. This is because generalization cannot be confirmed if evaluation data is used for learning or adjusted during the change process. The final check is done only once, with data that has never been seen during the experiment. If you check and adjust the same data multiple times, the results will be tailored to that data.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principles, let’s look at a detailed table of experiments applying the changes one by one.

screens.title: Experiment table with changes applied one by one
screens.lead: In the table, see how your experiment is configured to apply only one change per step. Take a look at what each step is trying to determine.

data.notes: Each step uses the results of the previous step as a new baseline. This way, at each step, you can read which changes had an effect on which axis. For example, adding examples changes consistency, adding search context changes factual accuracy, and tuning looks at consistency of format and tone. In actual work, order changes that are likely to be low-cost and high-impact first, and record the evaluation results at each stage. As the number of steps increases, the record becomes more valuable. It is enough to write down the experiment number, changes, and evaluation values ​​line by line.

screens.outro: Even if the experiment table was followed, there are limitations to interpretation. We will check in the next screen.

screens.title: Limitations of reproducibility and interpretation of results
screens.lead: Discover the mechanisms for switching between two states to make the results reliable, as well as the limitations in interpreting the results.

states.label: Reproducibility
states.body:
Reproducibility is the property of producing similar results when running the same settings again. Model outputs are non-deterministic, so the same input can result in different results, and the behavior changes as the model snapshot changes. So, take note of which model version you used.

It also records sampling settings such as seed and temperature. If possible, repeat the same assessment several times to see how scattered the results are. By knowing the scatter, you can determine whether the difference after the change is greater than the scatter. By recording your settings, you can recreate the baseline under the same conditions several weeks later. Even if team members change, you can continue in the same way.

states.label: Limitations of interpretation
states.body:
Experimental results are valid only within the evaluation set and settings. The results cannot be generalized to inputs outside the evaluation set. The extent of generalization depends on how well the evaluation set represents the operational input.

Rather than making a conclusion based on a single evaluation value difference, it is confirmed through repetition and decomposition by type. When reporting results, include which evaluation set and setting they were obtained from and how much you can and cannot say. As operations introduce new types of inputs, augment the evaluation set and re-baseline.

screens.outro: Let us now apply the principle through an example.

screens.title: Case commentary: When you can't come to a conclusion by changing three things at once
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case. Click the Next button to see why we can't come to a conclusion.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: When one team modified prompts, cleaned data, and tuned hyperparameters all at once, their evaluation value went up. The team decided to keep all three.

steps.title: Scenario A
steps.body: In reality, only the prompt modification had an effect, and the other two may have been unrelated. In this case, the time spent cleaning data and tuning hyperparameters was wasted without effect.

steps.title: Scenario B
steps.body: Data cleaning may have significantly increased the value, and hyperparameter tuning may have shaved off some of it. In this case, reverting the hyperparameters makes it even better. This possibility cannot be known by looking at the combined results alone.

steps.title: can't tell
steps.body: The effects of the three changes are mixed together, making it impossible to tell which scenario is which. I only know that the results have improved, but I cannot explain how they have improved.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Improvements whose effects cannot be explained cannot be used in the next task. Even if you try to make similar improvements to other features, you won't know which part is key and you'll have to try again from the beginning.

screens.outro: This time, we will see how to isolate the same situation and run it again.

screens.title: Case study: take it apart and run it again
screens.lead: The instructor shows how to reframe the previous example into a correct experiment. Click the next button to follow the steps.

steps.title: 1 Set priorities
steps.body: List the changes in the order they appear to have the lowest cost and highest impact. Prompt modifications are low-cost, so leave changes that require learning first first.

steps.title: 2 Compare alone
steps.body: Each change is applied independently and compared to the baseline. At this time, the evaluation set, grader, and sampling settings are all kept the same. Since there is only one change, the difference lies in that change. Evaluating each change once takes more time, but the information you get is much clearer.

steps.title: 3 Accumulate only effective changes
steps.body: Accumulate only the changes that are confirmed to be effective, and record an evaluation for each accumulation. Ineffective or rather cutting changes are filtered out at this stage.

steps.title: 4 Interaction is confirmed through combination
steps.body: If two changes are suspected to affect each other, only the combination of the two changes is compared further. Reduce costs by checking only suspect suspects rather than trying all combinations.

steps.title: 5 Leave a result table
steps.body: We leave a result table containing the effects and limitations of each change. This table becomes the basis for your next decision: what to keep and what to discard. It also serves as a reference when applying the same prescription elsewhere. In the result table, write down the changes, evaluation values, evaluation sets and settings used line by line.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of comparative experimental design. As you read, look back to see if there have been any recent changes.

paragraphs: Change only one thing at a time. The baseline that serves as the comparison group is run together, and the evaluation set, scorer, and sampling settings are fixed and recorded. You need these three things to be able to attribute the difference to change.

Model output is non-deterministic and behavior changes as model versions change, so check reproducibility and repeat as necessary. We also write down the limitations of interpretation that the results are only valid within the evaluation set and setting.
Isolating the change may seem to take longer, but knowing the cause will speed up the next steps. Only improvements that can demonstrate effectiveness become assets that can be transferred elsewhere.

Going back to the original question, the result of changing four things at once seems good, but I can't explain it. Only the results compared, one at a time, under the same conditions, serve as the basis for subsequent decisions.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Not all changes are independent of each other. Additional comparisons of combinations only when an interaction is suspected balances cost and accuracy. Leave your experiment records in a place where the team can see them together.

checks.intro: Think of an experimentation flow where you apply changes one by one. Just arrange the items in the appropriate order.
checks.q: Lay out the order of your experiments, applying changes one by one
items: Measure your baseline with default prompts
Just add few-shot examples to see changes in consistency.
Just add search context to see changes in factual accuracy
Replace with tuning model only to see format and tone consistency
checks.explain: Each step changes only one thing at a time and uses the result of the previous step as the new baseline.
checks.correctFeedback: The experiment table was ordered correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Start by taking a baseline and rearrange it into a flow that adds changes one at a time.

checks.intro: Think back to the case narrative. Just choose the most appropriate method for how to interpret the results.
checks.q: When I modified the prompt, cleaned the data, and adjusted the hyperparameters all at once, the index went up. How should we view these results?
options: You don't need to know the cause of the effect because you just need to maintain all three.
Since it is impossible to determine which changes were effective and cannot be used in the next task, the changes must be divided and compared again.
Since data organization is the most important, we conclude that it is thanks to data organization.
Since the index has risen, there is no need to check reproducibility.
checks.explain: If multiple changes are mixed, it may be difficult to tell which scenario is which, and some changes may have been undercut. It is correct to separate the changes and compare them alone to the baseline.

wrong.0: If you don't know the cause, there is no basis to reverse it or apply it elsewhere when it gets worse.
wrong.2: The share of data cleaning cannot be determined separately from the combined results.
wrong.3: Model output is non-deterministic and must be repeated to ensure reproducibility.

checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Improvements whose effectiveness cannot be explained should be isolated and compared again.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The fact that an indicator has risen is different from knowing the cause. Reconsider what follow-up action is needed in this gap.

glossary.def: It involves fixing conditions other than the factors you want to compare.
This is an experimental group run with unchanged baseline settings.
This is a property that produces similar results when reused with the same settings.
The limitation is that conclusions cannot be expanded beyond the evaluation set and settings.

misconceptions.myth: Since time is precious, it is more efficient to change several things at once.
misconceptions.fact: If you don't know the cause, the next step will be blocked and even slower. You need to be able to explain the effect so you can use it elsewhere.

misconceptions.myth: Once it goes up, it's confirmed.
misconceptions.fact: Model output fluctuates and needs to be checked repeatedly. See if the difference is greater than the scatter.

misconceptions.myth: As long as the numbers are correct, the comparison is valid.
misconceptions.fact: If you don't have the same evaluation set and settings fixed, you won't be able to put the numbers side by side.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Change only one thing at a time.
Set up a comparison group and fixed conditions.
Also note the limitations of interpretation of the results.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If some of our recent changes were made all at once, how can we break them down and compare them again?
